[CFO]: Thanks for the discussion today. For the record, can you send me a short note (just a couple of sentences) summarizing what’s behind the SMB churn pattern we saw in April/May and why you don’t see it as a structural issue?

[VP of the Business Line]: Just got this note from the CFO.

[VP of the Business Line]: Overall, the session went well — the growth and logo story landed, and your talking points on the miss and churn were helpful.

[VP of the Business Line]: Can you please draft 2–3 plain-English sentences I can drop straight into a reply email to the CFO that (a) restate the key drivers of the SMB churn optics and (b) underline why we see it as measurement/timing-heavy rather than a fundamental demand problem? Keep it fully consistent with the final deck, the $198.4M corporate total, and what we already said in the room; no new charts or numbers, just tight written language.

[VP of the Business Line]: Send me the exact text I should paste — I’d like to respond within the next 20–30 minutes.
rounds.response: The April–May SMB churn spike is primarily a measurement/timing effect driven by a mid‑quarter change in our logo‑churn definition and regional timing/consolidation, which temporarily raised reported churn in those months rather than reflecting a broad increase in customer losses. Core demand and engagement metrics — and the enterprise strength that produced our $198.4M topline — remain healthy, and we’ve launched targeted SMB retention and onboarding actions; the appendix contains the churn timeline and methodology if you’d like line‑level detail.
